chunk_findings.detail: `whole(repo, s)` is a check-then-act guard, and the content it validates is not the content that gets committed. It is evaluated for each shard in the list comprehension, but the bytes that end up in the blob are read again later: once by `W.git(repo, "add", "--", *shards)` and again by `W.git(repo, "commit", "-q", "-m", message, "--", *shards)` (and `git commit -- <pathspec>` records the *current working-tree* content of the named paths, not the blob staged a moment earlier). Concrete interleaving: shard `.ddflow/events/<id>.jsonl` currently ends with complete lines, so `whole()` returns True and the shard enters `shards`; between that read and the `git add`/`git commit` spawn, a concurrent writer (an agent appending directly with `>>`, i.e. a writer that holds no lock, which is exactly the case `whole()` exists to cover — if the writer took the lock `_busy(repo)` would already have refused) flushes only a prefix of a large event line into the file; `git add`/`git commit -- <path>` then stage and publish that half line. The result is precisely what the docstring promises to prevent — "a line nobody can read" — now permanently in the log that is described as the source of truth. The window also spans the `_busy(repo)` call, since the guard runs before it, so it is not narrowed by the lock check. The guard should re-verify (or hash/snapshot) the shard at commit time, or hold the log lock across `whole()` → `add` → `commit`, rather than trusting the earlier read.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/eventcommit.py:commit_shards (whole() guard)

chunk_findings.detail: The hook extracts the knob value with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` and then matches it against `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. The config dump in this same diff renders string-valued knobs with surrounding quotes — the golden snapshot shows `log.pre_push_events = 'warn'   [default]`, and `log.commit_events_message = 'events: {reason}'` likewise. For a line in that format, `$3` is `'warn'` (with the literal single quotes), so the `case` never matches `warn`, `block` or `off`; `mode` stays at its initialized `warn` and the `block`/`off` branches are dead code. Concretely: a project that sets `[log].pre_push_events = "block"` and pushes with uncommitted `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl` gets only a warning and the push succeeds, contradicting the documented guarantee that `block` makes a push never leave shards out; a project that sets `off` still gets the warning. (The same failure occurs if the emitted line carries the indentation shown in the snapshot, since the `^log\.` anchor then matches nothing and `m` is empty, again leaving `mode=warn`.) This also means the documented "unrecognised value ... falls back to 'block', the strictest" is not what the hook does — any value it cannot parse degrades to `warn`. The extraction needs to strip quotes (e.g. `sed "s/'//g"`/`tr -d "'"`) and tolerate indentation rather than assuming a bare `$3`.

chunk_findings.detail: The test proves "warn does not block the push" only by asserting the literal token `refused` is absent from stderr. A pre-push hook exits non-zero to abort the push, so the real property is `returncode == 0`; this assertion never checks it. Concretely, an implementation whose warn branch prints `... not committed ... (warning)` and then `sys.exit(1)` (or otherwise returns 1) blocks every push while still containing `"not committed"` in stderr and no `"refused"` token — the test passes although the default mode is blocking. The test should assert `p.returncode == 0` in addition to the message check.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_events_committed_doors.py::test_pre_push_warn_mode_does_not_refuse_for_the_shards

chunk_findings.detail: The test only asserts that the warning text is absent from stderr; it never checks the exit status. An `off` mode that crashes or is misparsed (e.g. the config lookup fails and the hook exits 1 without printing `not committed`) passes this test while silently aborting every push. Asserting `p.returncode == 0` would make the "off means the hook does nothing" contract testable.

Answers (AskUserQuestion, 2026-10-12): safeguard = a separate safeguard kind; weakening = an agent may weaken its own task's scope (with a reason), everything else operator; card cache = committed; lesson duty = warn by default

data.decision: Operator 2026-10-12 (AskUserQuestion). (1) A safeguard is its own record kind (trigger, audience, action, params, envelope), declared on the shared RecordKind descriptor like every kind: its own CLI group (ddflow safeguard) and ONE MCP tool (ddflow_safeguard, verbs as actions), with list, show, add, edit, remove, history, supersede, merge, split and restore from the record contract; a safeguard may cite the rules, decisions and lessons it came from; rules stay text. (2) WEAKENING: the operator may weaken, disable, remove or widen anything. An AGENT may waive a safeguard only for the ONE item it holds, with a reason: a task-scoped waiver recorded as an event, shown in the brief and by ddflow controls, expiring when the item completes or is released; a safeguard marked non_waivable (for example ask before pushing) cannot be waived by an agent; everything wider needs the operator and is held until acknowledged. This is a deliberate narrow exception to D-decision-management (waivers of decisions and goals stay operator-only). (3) CARDS (style and API) are COMMITTED to the repository (.ddflow/cards/, one file per card keyed by package and version or by config digest, so two branches rarely touch one file), regenerated from lock files and tool configs, declared as regenerated paths (no lease conflicts, regenerate after a merge, never text-merged), with size caps as knobs. (4) LESSON DUTY: closing a bug warns when no lesson is recorded (add one or pass --no-lesson --reason; the reason is logged); lessons.require_lesson_on_bug = off|warn|block, default warn. All values are knobs and every change is logged (D-everything-configurable).

data.body: D-safeguards (operator 2026-10-12): a SAFEGUARD IS ITS OWN RECORD KIND, not an extension of rules. Fields: id, title, text (short, token-capped), trigger (session_start|claim|dispatch|gate:<id>|pre_tool|pre_commit|merge), audience (agent, role, harness, model tier, subagent), action (inject|consult|require_ack|require_approval|refuse|cap), params, envelope (allowed_tools, allowed_skills, write_globs, max_turns, max_tokens, max_spend), non_waivable flag, cites (rule, decision and lesson ids it came from), status. Declared on the RecordKind descriptor (P-record-contract): CLI group ddflow safeguard, ONE MCP tool ddflow_safeguard (verbs as actions, tool-budget aware), list/show/add/edit/remove/history/supersede/merge/split/restore from the contract. A refuse or cap action needs a trigger the harness ladder can enforce, else it is stored with a 'cannot enforce here' note per harness (never treated as active). Rules stay plain text and keep their verbs; ddflow safeguard import-rule turns a rule into a safeguard when the user asks. Knobs: [safeguards] default trigger, max injected size per door, which actions an agent may add (stricter only).

data.body: ddflow controls [--for session|lane|item|agent] shows, in one table: active safeguards (and where each came from), subagent definitions and their envelopes, skills in force, last delivery, last change (who, when, why, prompt), cost per entry (tokens always loaded, last dispatch spend, tier). controls explain <session> answers 'what governed this session and why'. One engine behind CLI and MCP; edits go through the owning verbs (safeguard, rule, agent, skill), never a second write path; every row links to its history.

A subagent, skill or role definition carries an optional envelope: allowed_tools, allowed_skills, write_globs (default the item's globs, B-sub-sod), max_turns, max_tokens, max_spend (tokens and turns first, as D-gap-defaults). It is WRITTEN into the harness agent file where the harness supports tools/permission fields (descriptor-driven), TOLD in the dispatch brief everywhere, ENFORCED by flags when ddflow launches the agent (P-agent-parity.launcher: --max-turns), and CHECKED after the fact against the usage ledger (B-gap-spend) with a doctor note when exceeded. Widening an envelope is operator-only (B-sub-trust); the only agent relaxation is the one-item waiver of P-safeguards.waiver.

Exact numbers and rules, not paraphrase: 'line length 100, double quotes, import order isort, no print' read from [tool.ruff] and friends, one short card per language and path scope, delivered at claim and dispatch through the safeguard inject path; regenerated when the config digest changes; the standards gate checks the same configs, so the agent sees before writing what the gate enforces after. No network, no companion needed. CACHE (operator 2026-10-12): cards are COMMITTED under .ddflow/cards/, one file per card keyed by package and version (api) or config digest (style), so two branches rarely touch one file; declared as regenerated paths (no lease conflicts; regenerate after a merge, never text-merge: P-change-surface.pins concept); size caps are knobs.

Detect imports in the item's globs (Python ast first, JS/TS next) and pinned versions from uv.lock, poetry.lock, requirements, package-lock; a card is the few symbols the item likely uses: signature, one-line usage, 'changed or deprecated since', with provenance (source, retrieved, version) and size caps (knobs); stored in a cache keyed by package, version and symbol set, invalidated on a lock change; sources in order: the installed package's own docstrings and --help, project docs, llms.txt, a companion (context7) when one is reachable. A card says UNAVAILABLE when no source answered, never a guess. ddflow safeguard waive <id> --item <held item> --reason ... (CLI and MCP, same verb): an event safeguard.waived {safeguard, item, agent, reason}, only for an item the caller holds a live lease on, refused for a non_waivable safeguard (exit 3, explained), shown in the brief, by ddflow controls and in the dispatch brief, expires at complete, release or abandon, never carries over to another item or agent. Everything wider (disable, remove, edit, widen an envelope, waive for several items) is held for the operator. A deliberate narrow exception to D-decision-management (waivers of decisions stay operator-only). Regression: a waiver on one item does not weaken the same safeguard on another.

chunk_findings.detail: The hook reads the knob with `awk '/^log\.pre_push_events/ {print $3}'` and then matches that against `case "$m" in warn|block|off)`. The config dump this same change ships renders string knobs with surrounding quotes — the README knob table added by this diff literally lists `| log.pre_push_events | "warn" | ... |` and `| log.commit_events_message | "events: {reason}" |`, and the golden snapshot shows `log.pre_push_events = 'warn' [default]`. For such a line `$3` is `'warn'` (quotes included), which matches none of `warn|block|off`; the mode is therefore never set from config, so `block` cannot block a push and the intended `off`/`warn` semantics are lost. Nothing in the visible diff changes the awk expression or the rendering pipeline, so the mismatch stands.

chunk_findings.detail: `whole(repo, s)` is a check-then-act guard, and the bytes it validates are not the bytes committed: the content is re-read by `git add -- *shards` and again by `git commit -- *shards`, and `git commit -- <pathspec>` records the *current working-tree* content of the named paths, not the blob staged moments earlier. A concurrent writer that appends to a shard between the `whole()` check and the `commit` lands a shard whose last line does not parse (the very case `whole()` exists to skip) inside the event commit. The diff does not add a re-validation or a snapshot of the staged content, so the guard remains racy.

chunk_findings.detail: The event-log commit is issued before the after-merge check: `committed = EC.commit_at(log, cfg, "merge", f"merge {item}")` sits immediately above `ci_after = check_after_merge(repo, sha=sha, item=item, agent=agent)`. `check_after_merge` is handed `item` and `agent`, i.e. it is the step that attributes/records the CI outcome for this merge in the event log, so it appends a shard under `.ddflow/events/`. Because the commit already ran, that shard is not part of the commit: after a normal merge whose after-merge check records its result, the primary checkout still has a dirty/untracked `.ddflow/events/*.jsonl`, so `doctor` still reports uncommitted shards and the pre-push hook still warns about main lacking shards present in the working tree — precisely the failure this change is supposed to fix. The intent says ddflow commits the shards it wrote "at merge/complete/release/stop", i.e. as the last event-producing step of the command; the call needs to move after `check_after_merge` (otherwise only the pre-CI shards are ever committed and every merge leaves new uncommitted shards behind).

data.question: How do subagents, parallel sessions and steering behave in opencode 1.19.0, probed on the real binary?

data.body: Falsifiable claims with a recorded probe each, Claude Code and Kilo first (both installed here), the rest from source and docs: (1) Kilo's task/subagent tool blocks the parent until the child session ends (operator-observed, mechanism unverified), while a second session via kilo serve plus prompt_async does not; (2) Claude Agent run_in_background returns at once and notifies on completion, SendMessage continues; (3) Codex spawn_agent: does it return immediately, how are messages sent to the agent, how is the result read; (4) Gemini subagents; (5) Cursor and Antigravity background agents; (6) Copilot cloud delegation; (7) Cline spawn/team. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. Differences to record separately: opencode lacks Kilo-only features (agent_manager tool, /goal, wakeup tools, session.turn events); opencode V2 (dev branch, 2.0.27) has an incompatible plugin and possibly different session API, so every [spawn] value for opencode carries a version range and the adapter is version-gated (opencode --version major 1 vs 2). PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. Still to probe: the same routes on Kilo 7.8.x (installed 7.2.20 is too old to show them), and a model-backed run to OBSERVE the blocking (needs a provider credential the operator supplies).

ddflow spawn steer|pause|resume|cancel|rescope <lane>: steer sends a message the child sees next (Kilo prompt_async queues while busy; Claude SendMessage; Codex message to the agent; ACP prompt where used; otherwise a lane.note the child receives through its change feed and the hook doors), pause and cancel abort the turn (Kilo abort endpoint, process signal for launched lanes) and keep or release the lease, resume restarts with the hand-off, rescope edits the item (globs, body, safeguards) and the child is told. Every verb is logged, a master may steer only its own children unless the operator says otherwise, and a harness that cannot do one says so (parity report). opencode/Kilo mechanics (probed on opencode 1.19.0): steer = POST /session/{id}/prompt_async (queues while busy), cancel = POST /session/{id}/abort or POST /api/session/{id}/interrupt, wait = POST /api/session/{id}/wait, state = GET /session/status and GET /api/session/active, children = GET /session/{id}/children, fork = POST /session/{id}/fork.

NAMING (2026-10-12): `ddflow lanes` (B-gap-lanes) is the READ-ONLY ledger and advisor of lanes: it lists lanes, their state and the exact spawn line, and never spawns. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. The opencode V2 plugin API (Plugin.define({id, setup(ctx)}), hooks under ctx.session.hook('prompt'|'context'|'compaction'|...)) replaces the v1 named hooks. Write the V2 implementation of the ddflow plugin (prompt capture, tool monitoring and enforcement, session id, handoff on compaction, stop-to-continue through the continuation engine) behind the same contract as the 1.x one, selected by 'opencode --version'; until V2 is the npm latest it is opt-in. data.question: Can ddflow run periodic and event-triggered work per project, fully managed by the user, for full-suite checks (duplication, bugs, security), dependency and partner-tool updates, and for ddflow itself keeping up with the coding agents?

data.body: R-schedule-reach: nothing watches partner tools, dependencies or the coding agents generically. A watch is a definition (.ddflow/watches/<id>.toml, log events like schedules, same validation and authoring verbs): source, how to read the current value, how to compare with the last seen, the job whose template files the item, a minimum interval, enabled. State is the last seen value, kept as watch.observed events so it replays and merges. A change files an item from the job template with the before/after and links; no change files nothing; an unreachable source is UNAVAILABLE and counted (a watch that is silent for N periods is itself a doctor note). Network use is operator-defined: allowed hosts are an operator-only knob; nothing is fetched from a committed config the operator did not approve. Rate limits and offline behaviour are knobs.
data.title: Watches: a generic upstream-change primitive (version, changelog, release feed, command output) that files research or upgrade items when something changes

data.body: One small module per source, registered by convention: npm, PyPI, crates.io, GitHub releases and tags, Docker tags, an installed tool's --version and --help digest (the agent CLIs, companions), the project's own outdated report (uv pip list --outdated, npm outdated, cargo outdated, go list -u), a changelog or docs page by content digest or feed. Each returns a value, a digest and a retrieved time; a failure says why. No credential in a committed file; keys from the environment only. Tests use recorded fixtures and a fake server, never the network.
data.title: Watch source adapters: package indexes, release feeds, installed CLI versions, lockfile outdated reports, changelog pages

data.body: Keeping up with an upstream tool is research, then a decision, then work. A chain template files the research item on a change (what changed, what it means for this project, a falsifiable claim and a probe), and on its completion a proposal or implementation tasks (P-observe.proposals), and a verification item (the live smoke or the conformance run) once those land. Stages are linked items, so the lease, gates and cross-family review apply to each; a chain has a budget and a cap on open stages; it never starts an agent by itself (D-trigger-actions-create-items).
data.title: Multi-stage jobs: watch -> research item -> adoption proposal -> verification, each stage an ordinary item with its own pipeline

data.body: D-sched-no-daemon means due-ness is computed but something else must start the work. An executor is registered per project (ddflow schedule executor add): a harness routine (Claude Code Routines, cron or /loop), an OpenClaw cron or heartbeat, a GitHub Actions workflow, a systemd timer or plain cron; the emitter prints exactly what to install (B-sched-emitters) and the executor's heartbeat is recorded so doctor can say 'job X was due 3 days ago and no executor has run' (the silent no-fire failure). The executor runs ddflow schedule due --run and then works the filed items through the lane launcher headless (P-agent-parity.launcher) with an unattended permission profile, spend and turn caps, quota guard (P-governor) and the operator's approval for merges of dependency, security and architecture changes. Report-only is the default mode.
data.title: Who works the queue when nobody is there: register an executor, emit its schedule, run headless with caps, and warn when a job is due and nothing will run it

data.body: Extends B-sched-defaults (security, dependency, architecture, duplication, CI health, SECURITY.md sync) with a catalogue chosen per project type (Python, JS, Rust, Go, ML repo): full-suite duplication sweep, whole-codebase bug audit, security audit and advisory check, dependency updates (grouped, never auto-merged), licence check, secret scan, dead code, doc freshness and link check, flaky-test quarantine, slow-test report, coverage trend, log backup verify, agent-config drift, release readiness. Every entry is data (a job plus a prompt), disabled by default except cheap report-only ones, and edited, disabled or deleted by the user with the same verbs; ddflow schedule init offers the set for the detected project type with the cost and frequency of each.
data.title: A library of project-type job templates chosen at onboarding: duplication, bug audit, security, dependencies, licences, secrets, dead code, doc freshness and links, flaky and slow tests, coverage, backup, agent-config drift

data.body: The concrete definitions this repository runs on itself (a project can copy them): a weekly watch over every supported agent CLI (--version, --help digest, release feed) that files a research item per change with the descriptor to re-verify; a monthly market re-scan for new agents; companion versions (roborev, codeguide, context7, memory); MCP spec and SDK versions; Python, uv, ruff and CI action versions; each chain ends in descriptor corrections, new parity features or a closed 'nothing to do' with the reason. P-agent-parity.drift becomes the agent-specific checks on top of this machinery, not a separate scheduler.

data.body: ddflow schedule history [id]: runs, outcome (ok, findings, failed, unavailable, budget-hit), items and bugs filed, duration, tokens or spend where known, and the yield (findings per run, accepted per filed). A job with zero yield over N runs is flagged and a slower cadence proposed (P-observe.proposals), a job that always finds something is flagged for a fix task; the circuit breaker of B-sched-run is the hard stop, this is the soft signal. Feeds P-observe.effect.
data.title: Job outcomes and yield: history, cost and findings per run, and a frequency suggestion when a job never finds anything

(1) AUTONOMY: ddflow detects and proposes, and may also TUNE BOUNDED KNOBS from the start: an allowlist with min, max, step and a rate limit per knob family, one experiment at a time per family, guardrail metrics measured independently of the target, a pre-registered window and stop rule, and automatic rollback when a guardrail breaches; every step is a config.changed event with the experiment id. (2) RETROSPECTIVES run on BOTH a different-family reviewer endpoint and the working agent, and the two are compared: where they disagree is reported, a proposal both make carries more weight, and each run is budgeted (token budget per run, weekly cap: knobs). (3) Not asked, defaults: no cross-project data leaves the machine; LLM-run moments are off until the operator enables them, cheap deterministic ones are on. All values are knobs (D-everything-configurable).

data.claim: In opencode 1.19.0 the task tool runs the subagent as a child session and the parent stays busy until the child finishes (blocking); the documented detach route did not free it in this setup; aborting the child does free the parent immediately
data.falsifier: the parent goes idle while the child still runs, or the detach route frees the parent
data.mechanism: task tool creates a child session observable at GET /session/{id}/children; /session/status shows the parent busy for the child's whole run; POST /experimental/session/{id}/background is documented to detach blocking subagents; POST /session/{child}/abort stops the child
data.probe: opencode-ai 1.19.0 in a scratch directory with isolated HOME; opencode serve --pure; free anonymous model opencode/big-pickle (no credential); a parent session prompted via prompt_async to use the task tool once for a subagent running 'sleep 35'; polled /session/status and /session/{id}/children every 2 s; run 1 called POST /experimental/session/{id}/background 8 s after the child appeared; run 2 called POST /session/{child}/abort; run 3 called POST /api/session/{parent}/interrupt
data.probe_output: run 1: child session appeared at 6 s, parent stayed busy from 2 s to 44 s, detach call at 14 s returned (200, false) and changed nothing, parent went idle at 46 s right after the child finished, final assistant text FINISHED; run 2: abort of the child returned (200, true) and both parent and child were idle within 2 s (the parent's turn ended too); run 3: INCONCLUSIVE (the model never started a child in that run, so interrupt was not exercised); my sleep-process counter was unreliable (it counted its own pgrep) and is discarded; free models listed without credentials: opencode/big-pickle, nemotron-3.5-lightning-free, ling-3.1-flash-free and others; Kilo not probed model-backed (installed 7.2.20 too old)
data.question: Does opencode 1.19.0 really block the parent session while a subagent runs, and which routes free it?

data.body: Falsifiable claims with a recorded probe each, Claude Code and Kilo first (both installed here), the rest from source and docs: (1) Kilo's task/subagent tool blocks the parent until the child session ends (operator-observed, mechanism unverified), while a second session via kilo serve plus prompt_async does not; (2) Claude Agent run_in_background returns at once and notifies on completion, SendMessage continues; (3) Codex spawn_agent: does it return immediately, how are messages sent to the agent, how is the result read; (4) Gemini subagents; (5) Cursor and Antigravity background agents; (6) Copilot cloud delegation; (7) Cline spawn/team. Each result lands in the descriptor's [spawn] section as data (blocking yes/no/unknown, background, steer, resume, abort, result retrieval, depth, isolation) with source and date. Unknown stays unknown. OPENCODE (added 2026-10-12): treat opencode 1.19 and Kilo as ONE engine family (Kilo is an opencode v1 fork; descriptor family = opencode) and probe once for both: the task/subagent tool's blocking behaviour, `opencode serve` + `opencode run --attach` / POST /session + prompt_async + /abort + GET /event for independent sessions, `opencode run -s/--fork/--share`, parallel sessions under one server. Differences to record separately: opencode lacks Kilo-only features (agent_manager tool, /goal, wakeup tools, session.turn events); opencode V2 (dev branch, 2.0.27) has an incompatible plugin and possibly different session API, so every [spawn] value for opencode carries a version range and the adapter is version-gated (opencode --version major 1 vs 2). PROBED 2026-10-12 (R-spawn-opencode-probe, opencode 1.19.0 installed in a scratch dir, isolated HOME): subagents are SYNCHRONOUS by default (the schema of POST /experimental/session/{id}/background says 'Detach any synchronous subagents currently blocking the session and continue them in the background'); subagents are child sessions (GET /session/{id}/children); parallel sessions under one server work; abort, interrupt, wait, prompt_async, /session/status and /api/session/active exist; `opencode acp` is an ACP server. Still to probe: the same routes on Kilo 7.8.x (installed 7.2.20 is too old to show them), and a model-backed run to OBSERVE the blocking (needs a provider credential the operator supplies). V2: the opencode dev build (0.0.0-dev-202610110139) has the same session routes (background, prompt_async, abort, interrupt, wait, children) as 1.19.0, so spawn, steer and detach need no V2 gate; only the plugin differs. OBSERVED 2026-10-13 (R-opencode-blocking-observed, free model, no credential): the opencode task tool BLOCKS the parent (busy 2 s to 44 s while the child ran 6 s to ~44 s); POST /experimental/session/{id}/background returned false and freed nothing; POST /session/{child}/abort freed the parent in about 2 s (its turn ended). Interrupt of the parent was not exercised. Kilo is still unprobed model-backed.

When the master is blocked waiting for a synchronous subagent (the opencode and Kilo default), the user or another door can run ddflow spawn detach [--session S]: for opencode 1.x it calls POST /experimental/session/{id}/background on the session's server (needs the server address: a ddflow plugin records it, or the session was started by the launcher), after which the child continues as a background lane the ledger shows and the master is free. Descriptor [spawn.native] detach = {route}. Where a harness has no detach, say so and offer abort (steer) or the independent-session route. Version-gated and experimental-flagged (the route is under /experimental): a failing call never harms the session. A plugin hook can also call it automatically after N minutes of a blocking child ([spawn] auto_detach_after_s, off by default). PROBE RESULT (R-opencode-blocking-observed): the experimental background route returned false on opencode 1.19.0 and did not detach, so it is NOT relied on: the verb tries it first (cheap, harmless) and then falls back to the verified route: POST /session/{child}/abort frees the parent within about 2 s; the child's work is then re-run as an independent lane (P-spawn.engine) with the same brief. Need to learn why the route returns false (a required experimental flag, or only valid from the TUI) before promising detach; that is the first step of this task.
data.title: Unblock a stuck master: ddflow spawn unblock frees a parent blocked on a subagent (detach where it works, otherwise cancel the child and relaunch it as an independent lane)

data.body: The driver and the MCP instructions say: delegate with ddflow spawn, not with a blocking subagent tool, for anything that may take more than a few minutes; do not sit in ddflow wait; check lanes or wait for the notice. harness verify flags a harness whose only native route blocks (Kilo's task tool, per the facts) and names the independent-session route. Honest limit: where a model ignores the instruction ddflow cannot stop it; the parity suite measures it. Evidence: opencode 1.19.0 task tool observed blocking the parent for the child's whole run; for long delegations use the independent-session route.

data.body: ddflow tell <lane|session|item|phase|glob|all> --text ... | --ref <record id> [--urgency fyi|next-door|safe-point|now]: a message.sent event (fenced, redacted, bounded) addressed by identity or scope. fyi and next-door ride the change feed (B-rc-changes) at the next door; safe-point is delivered between gates; now uses the harness steer route (P-spawn.steer) and is refused where none exists, saying so. CLI and one MCP tool, one declaration. Who may tell whom: the operator anyone, a master its children and peers on its items, an agent only its master; rate limits and size caps are knobs. A message is DATA to the receiver, never an approval or a permission change (D-session-context).

data.body: Placeholder dependency replaced below. On any edit of a rule, safeguard, decision, lesson, the item a lane holds (body, globs, needs), a quota or governor pause, or a plan change, compute from the lanes ledger (B-gap-lanes) which live lanes it governs (their item globs, audience, scope, phase) and classify: BLOCKING (a new prohibition or a pause: delivered at the next door with urgency safe-point or now), CHANGES-YOUR-TASK (item or acceptance edit), FYI. The edit command previews 'affects 3 lanes: ...' and notifies by default for BLOCKING (knob). Batches within a window so ten edits are one notice.

data.body: Each delivery of a brief, claim guidance or dispatch brief records a context revision for the lane: a digest over the ids and digests of the governing records (item text, safeguards, rules, decisions, lessons, cards). ddflow lanes shows STALE when the current revision differs; at the next door the lane gets a DELTA (what changed, bounded), not the whole brief, and a full re-brief at a safe point when the delta is large (knob). A lane on a harness with no doors is marked UNREACHABLE-WITHOUT-POLL so the master knows.
data.title: Stale-context marker: what each lane was last told, a revision of what governs it, and a delta when it changes

data.body: A receiver acknowledges implicitly (it called a door after delivery) or explicitly (ddflow ack). message.seen events give latency from send to seen; a BLOCKING notice unseen after N minutes (knob) is escalated: to the master, then to the operator through the ask engine (P-remote.ask), and the lane is marked as possibly working on stale rules. Harnesses with no door get an instruction to call a cheap pull (the existing ddflow_brief or ddflow_lanes with a since cursor, no new MCP tool, tool budget) at every task step. Honest limit: ddflow cannot force a model to read.
data.title: Acknowledgement and escalation: seen events, unacknowledged BLOCKING notices escalate to the master or user, and door-less harnesses poll cheaply

data.body: ddflow share post|read|list --scope item|phase|glob|topic: append-only, fenced, size-capped, TTL, dedupe, subscribed by scope so a lane touching the importer sees what another lane found there, delivered at the doors as FYI. 1. Is a principle a new kind or a field? DEFAULT: a field, not a kind. Add one field to the guidance record, override = none | waive | deviate (how a finding is cleared), orthogonal to enforcement (how hard a finding is). Principle = enforcement warn + override deviate; rule = block + waive; org floor = block + none; preference = advisory. Vocabulary shown to people: MUST / SHOULD / MAY (RFC 2119) next to the enforcement word. Rejected: a separate principle store (a second engine to keep in step), and enforcement alone (a warn finding needs no answer, so a soft rule fails by silence).
2. Who may deviate from a principle, and does it expire? DEFAULT: the authoring agent records a deviation, item-scoped, reason required (evidence optional), no approval, no expiry (it dies with the item), always visible in brief, completion summary and the operator's decision list. Only block rules need a person's waiver (up to 90 days, approved by digest, unchanged). A deviation from a principle on a CHECK-LESS record (judged by a reviewer) is accepted the same way.
3. Must a principle finding be answered before complete? DEFAULT: yes for SHOULD with a mechanical check or a reviewer finding that cites the id; complete refuses (exit 3) listing the unanswered ones; an answer is comply (fixed) or deviate (reason). 4. Precedence order. 5. Goal record shape. 6. What does the brief show of goals? DEFAULT: at most 3 lines (active goals by priority: title, mean KR progress, weakest KR, days to target, stale flag), plus at claim the item's goal chain (task -> phase -> goal) labelled Direction, not a constraint; orphan work (completed items under no goal) counted in the roadmap and doctor, never a gate.

DEFAULT: off. `[review.panel.<gate>]` members (reviewer names), min_members, verdict_rule (any_confirmed | majority | all), merge_floor (similarity for merging equal findings); every member must pass the independence rule; a panel with fewer than min_members available is partial/unavailable, never passed; the synthesis is the gate's record (one id for triage), each finding carries who found it and the agreement count.

10. Phase-level or task-level. DEFAULT: the claims review and the corpus checks run at the docs gate of a phase and in the docs-correctness schedule job; the scenario gate is task-level only when added.
